# Attack 11 — Hodge classes on powers $X^k$ and Mumford–Tate groups

**Verdict in one paragraph.** The top target (a), read literally ("if $\mathrm{MT}(X)$ is as large as the polarization and endomorphisms allow, the Hodge classes on all powers $X^k$ are generated by Künneth components, diagonals, polarizations and endomorphisms"), is **false**, as already observed for K3 surfaces by Varesco [Var24, §0.1, Thm. 2.16]; we give the general mechanism (Proposition 2.3, Theorem A(5)). Because $\mathrm{MT}(X)$ is connected, "as large as allowed" can only mean that $\mathrm{Hg}(X)$ is the *identity component* $G_S^0$ of the group $G_S$ fixing the structural algebraic classes $S$. In general $G_S$ is disconnected. Its component group is detected by **orientation classes** $o_i(X)\in\Lambda^{b_i}H^i(X,\mathbb Q)\subset H^{ib_i}(X^{b_i},\mathbb Q)$. For every $X$ these are Hodge classes (Proposition 2.2). A reflection in $G_S$ moves them, so they never lie in the tensor span of $S$. What is proved here: (1) the Tannakian criterion and its $\pi_0$-refinement under the Lefschetz standard conjecture $B$ (§1). These are formal and known in substance. (2) **Theorem A**: let $H^*(X)$ be "algebraic classes $\oplus$ one generic piece $V$ in middle degree $n$". If $n$ is odd, HC holds for all $X^k$. If $n$ is even, HC holds for $X^k$ when $k<\dim V$, and HC for all powers is *equivalent* to the algebraicity of the single class $o_V$ on $X^{\dim V}$. This covers surfaces with $p_g=1$, $q=0$, $\mathrm{End}_{HS}(T)=\mathbb Q$; for K3 surfaces this is in substance Varesco's theorem. It also covers very general hypersurfaces. (3) **Theorem B**: the Kuga–Satake Hodge conjecture for a surface $S$ with $p_g=1$ implies that $o_{T(S)}$ is algebraic, for every Picard number. The proof uses only one endomorphism of the Kuga–Satake variety (left multiplication by the Clifford volume element), and no Hodge conjecture on its powers. (4) **Theorem C**: an unconditional reduction, via Weyl's polarization theorem, of HC for all powers of *any* $X$ to finitely many explicit Hodge classes. (5) **Proposition 6.2**: for $2d$-polarized K3 surfaces, HC for all powers of the very general member is equivalent to a bounded-degree (variational) statement for one flat class over the orientation double cover of moduli. Seeds exist at all CM points. **Not proved:** the algebraicity of $o_T$ for any K3 surface with $\mathrm{End}(T)=\mathbb Q$ that is not covered by known Kuga–Satake results (in particular the very general one). This is the top of rung (b). Lemma 6.1 proves that no family of cycles defined over the whole moduli space can produce it. Gaps: §7. Checklist: §8.

**Referee (2026-11-13):** minor revision; corrections applied. Report summary: docs/06-attack-report.md.

## 0. Conventions and standing facts

$X$ is smooth projective over $\mathbb C$, $n=\dim X$, $H:=H^*(X,\mathbb Q)=\bigoplus_iH^i$, $b_i=\dim H^i$. Künneth identifies $H^*(X^k,\mathbb Q)=H^{\otimes k}$ (graded tensor product). Permutations of factors act with Koszul signs, and the exterior product $\alpha\times\beta=pr_1^*\alpha\cup pr_2^*\beta$ corresponds to $\alpha\otimes\beta$. "Algebraic" means: in the $\mathbb Q$-span of classes of algebraic cycles; $A^*(Y)$ denotes the algebraic classes on $Y$. $GL^{gr}(H)=\prod_iGL(H^i)$ acts on $H^{\otimes k}$ diagonally. For a set $S$ of classes on powers of $X$, $G_S\subset GL^{gr}(H)$ is its pointwise stabilizer.

**Fact 0.1 (Hodge group).** Let $\mathrm{Hg}(X)\subset GL^{gr}(H)$ be the smallest $\mathbb Q$-algebraic subgroup whose real points contain $h(U(1))$. It is connected, and it is reductive because each $H^i$ is polarizable. *This is the first place where projectivity is used* [Del82, §3]. A class on $X^k$ (of any degree) is a Hodge class (each component of degree $2p$ is of type $(p,p)$, and odd-degree components vanish) iff it is $\mathrm{Hg}(X)$-invariant. Reason: $z\in U(1)$ acts on $H^{p,q}$ by $z^{q-p}$, and the stabilizer of a rational vector is a $\mathbb Q$-group.

**Fact 0.2 [Del82, Prop. 3.1(c)].** A reductive $G\subset GL(W)$ is the subgroup fixing all $G$-invariants in all $W^{\otimes a}\otimes W^{\vee\otimes b}$. By noetherianity, finitely many invariants suffice. An element of $GL^{gr}(H)$ fixing $[\Delta_X]$ is an isometry for Poincaré duality (PD), so PD transports mixed tensors to $H^{\otimes k}$ equivariantly. Hence $\mathrm{Hg}(X)$ is the pointwise stabilizer in $GL^{gr}(H)$ of the Hodge classes on all $X^k$, and finitely many of these suffice.

**Fact 0.3 (correspondences [Ful98, Ch. 16]).** For $\Gamma\in A^*(Y\times Z)$, $\Gamma_*x=pr_{Z*}(\Gamma\cup pr_Y^*x)$ preserves algebraicity. We have $\int_Z\Gamma_*x\cup y=\pm\int_Yx\cup({}^t\Gamma)_*y$. Composites act by composites. Künneth projectors are algebraic for surfaces [Mur90] and abelian varieties [Lie68, DM91].

**Fact 0.4 (first fundamental theorems [Wey39, Ch. II]; [GW09, Ch. 5]).** Let $W$ be a vector space over a field of characteristic 0 with a nondegenerate form $\psi$, and let $\psi^{-1}\in W\otimes W$ be the inverse tensor. For a perfect matching $\mu$ of $\{1,\dots,m\}$, write $\psi^{-1}_\mu\in W^{\otimes m}$ for copies of $\psi^{-1}$ placed on the pairs of $\mu$.
- **(Sp)** If $\psi$ is alternating, $(W^{\otimes m})^{Sp(W)}$ is spanned by the $\psi^{-1}_\mu$.
- **(O)** If $\psi$ is symmetric, $(W^{\otimes m})^{O(W)}$ is spanned by the $\psi^{-1}_\mu$.
- **(SO)** If $\psi$ is symmetric and $r=\dim W\ge3$, let $\delta$ span $\Lambda^rW\subset W^{\otimes r}$. Then $(W^{\otimes m})^{SO(W)}$ is spanned by the $\psi^{-1}_\mu$ together with the tensors $\delta_J\otimes\psi^{-1}_\mu$, where $|J|=r$ and $\mu$ is a matching of the complement; the latter occur only when $m\ge r$ and $m\equiv r\pmod 2$. (A product of two determinants is a polynomial in $\psi$.)

These statements are classical over $\overline{\mathbb Q}$. The spanning tensors are rational, and invariants commute with field extension, so the statements hold over $\mathbb Q$.

**Fact 0.5 (Weyl's polarization theorem [KP96, §7.1]; [DKW08]).** Let $G$ be any group acting linearly on $W$, $\dim W=N$, in characteristic 0. If $\{f_j\}$ generates $K[W^{\oplus N}]^G$, then for $m\ge N$ the polarizations of the $f_j$ generate $K[W^{\oplus m}]^G$. Here a polarization of $f_j$ is a multihomogeneous component of $(w_1,\dots,w_m)\mapsto f_j(\sum_lA_{1l}w_l,\dots,\sum_lA_{Nl}w_l)$ for some $A\in M_{N\times m}(K)$.

**Fact 0.6 (Zarhin [Zar83, Thms. 1.5.1, 2.2.1, 2.3.1]).** Let $T$ be an irreducible polarized Hodge structure of K3 type and $E=\mathrm{End}_{HS}(T)$. Then $E$ is totally real or CM, and $\mathrm{Hg}(T)=SO_E(T)$, resp. $U_E(T)$. In particular $E=\mathbb Q\Rightarrow\mathrm{Hg}(T)=SO(T,q)$.

## 1. The formal part of (a): Tannakian criterion (known in substance)

Let $G_{alg}(X)\subset GL^{gr}(H)$ be the set of $g$ such that $g^{\otimes k}$ fixes every algebraic class on $X^k$, for every $k$. Algebraic classes are Hodge classes, so $\mathrm{Hg}(X)\subset G_{alg}(X)$.

**Proposition 1.1 (known: [Jan92], [DM82], [And96a], [And04, Ch. 6–7]).** Assume $B(X)$. Then, for every $k$, the algebraic classes on $X^k$ are exactly the $G_{alg}(X)$-invariants of $H^{\otimes k}$. Hence the following are equivalent: HC for $X^k$ for all $k$; $\mathrm{Hg}(X)=G_{alg}(X)$; there is a finite set $S$ of algebraic classes on powers of $X$ with $G_S=\mathrm{Hg}(X)$.

*Proof.* $B(X)$ implies $B(X^k)$ for all $k$, hence the Künneth conjecture $C(X^k)$, and, in characteristic 0 (Hodge index), $D(X^k)$, i.e. homological equivalence equals numerical equivalence [Kle68, Kle94, Lie68]. Let $\mathcal M$ be the pseudo-abelian rigid tensor category of homological motives generated by $h(X)$, with objects $(X^k,p,m)$. By $D$ and [Jan92] it is abelian and semisimple. Modify the commutativity constraint by the (algebraic) Künneth projectors. Then Betti cohomology $\mathsf H$ becomes an exact faithful tensor functor, so $\mathcal M\simeq\mathrm{Rep}(G_{hom})$ with $G_{hom}=\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}^\otimes(\mathsf H)$ [DM82, Thm. 2.11]. The Lefschetz motive $L$ is the summand of $h(X)$ cut out by $(\int h^n)^{-1}h^{n-1}\times h$, so $G_{hom}\subset GL(H)$. Let $\chi$ be the character of $G_{hom}$ on $\mathsf H(L)$ and $G^1=\ker\chi$.

(i) $G^1=G_{alg}$. Elements of $G_{hom}$ act on algebraic classes of degree $2p$ by $\chi^p$, so $G^1\subset G_{alg}$. Conversely, let $g\in G_{alg}$. Then $g$ fixes $[pt]$, so it preserves $\int$. It fixes $[\Delta_X]$, so it is a PD-isometry. It fixes the small diagonal $[\Delta_3]\in H^{\otimes3}$, which represents $(x,y,z)\mapsto\int x\cup y\cup z$; therefore $g$ is a ring automorphism of $H$. Hence each $g^{\otimes k}$ is a ring automorphism of $H^*(X^k)$ preserving $\int$, and it commutes with every algebraic correspondence, because it fixes the correspondence and push-forward is adjoint to pull-back. Letting $g$ act trivially on $\mathbb Q(1)$ gives an element of $\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}^\otimes(\mathsf H)$ with $\chi=1$.

(ii) By Tannakian duality, the algebraic classes in $H^{2p}(X^k)$ are $\mathrm{Hom}(1,h(X^k)(p))=\{t:gt=\chi(g)^pt\ \forall g\in G_{hom}\}$. The weight cocharacter $w$ ($s^i$ on $H^i$) lies in $G_{hom}$ because the Künneth projectors are morphisms, and $\chi(w(s))=s^2$, so $G_{hom}=G^1\cdot w(\mathbb G_m)$. Let $t$ be a $G^1$-invariant of degree $j$. Since $w(-1)\in G^1$, we get $t=(-1)^jt$, so $j$ is even. Then $g_1w(s)t=s^{j}t=\chi(g_1w(s))^{j/2}t$, so $t$ is algebraic.

(iii) If $\mathrm{Hg}=G_{alg}$, the Hodge classes are the $\mathrm{Hg}$-invariants, which are the $G_{alg}$-invariants, which are algebraic. If all Hodge classes are algebraic, then $G_{alg}$ fixes all of them, so $G_{alg}\subset\mathrm{Hg}$ by Fact 0.2; the same fact provides a finite $S$. Conversely, if $G_S=\mathrm{Hg}$ with $S$ algebraic, then $G_{alg}\subset G_S=\mathrm{Hg}\subset G_{alg}$. $\square$

**Proposition 1.2 ($\pi_0$-refinement).** Assume $B(X)$. Let $S$ be a set of algebraic classes on powers of $X$, containing $[pt]$ and the small diagonals, such that $G_S^0=\mathrm{Hg}(X)$. For each component $c\ne1$ of $G_S$ (over $\overline{\mathbb Q}$), choose a rational Hodge class $u_c$ on some $X^{k_c}$ that is moved by $c$; such a class exists. Then HC holds for all $X^k$ iff the finitely many classes $u_c$ are algebraic.

*Proof.* Elements of one component differ by elements of $\mathrm{Hg}$, so they act identically on Hodge classes. Each $\gamma\notin\mathrm{Hg}(\overline{\mathbb Q})$ moves some Hodge class over $\overline{\mathbb Q}$ (Fact 0.2), hence moves a rational one, since rational Hodge classes span. We have $\mathrm{Hg}\subset G_{alg}\subset G_S$, so $G_{alg}$ is a union of components. If every $u_c$ is algebraic, no component $c\neq1$ lies in $G_{alg}$, so $G_{alg}=\mathrm{Hg}$; conclude by Proposition 1.1. The converse is trivial. $\square$

**Remark 1.3 (what is, and is not, new relative to André, Tankeev, Murty–Hazama–Milne).**

*Abelian varieties.* For an abelian variety $A$, take $S$ to be the polarization and $\mathrm{End}^0(A)$ (divisor classes on $A\times A$). Adding $[pt]$, $[\Delta_A]$ and the small diagonal (so that $G_S$ acts by ring automorphisms, i.e. through $GL(H^1)$), $G_S$ is the Lefschetz group $L(A)$, the centralizer of $\mathrm{End}^0(A)$ in $Sp$. The Lefschetz classes are the $L(A)$-invariants [Mil99]. All Hodge classes on all powers are Lefschetz iff $\mathrm{Hg}(A)=L(A)$ [Mur84, Haz85]; Tankeev and Ribet prove $\mathrm{Hg}=L$ for simple abelian varieties of prime dimension [Tan82, Rib83]. In this language those theorems are the case "$G_S$ connected and equal to $\mathrm{Hg}$". When $A$ has type III, $L(A)$ has an orthogonal factor and is disconnected. Murty's exceptional classes are then the abelian prototype of the orientation classes of §2.

*André.* All Hodge classes on products of abelian varieties and K3 surfaces are motivated [And96a, And96b], so the motivated analogue of rung (b) holds unconditionally. Motivated cycles use the Lefschetz involution of auxiliary varieties, such as compactified total spaces of families, where $B$ is unknown. What this file adds is the exact location of the gap between "motivated" and "algebraic" on all powers. For $\mathrm{End}(T)=\mathbb Q$ that gap is the single class $o_T$ (Corollary 3.1).

*Claims of novelty.* Propositions 1.1 and 1.2 are formal and are not claimed as new. The claims are limited to §2 (in this generality), Theorem A beyond K3 surfaces, Theorem B, Theorem C as stated, and §6.

## 2. Orientation classes: the obstruction to the literal top target

**Definition 2.1.** Let $V\subset H^i(X,\mathbb Q)$ be a sub-Hodge structure with $v=\dim V>0$. Its **orientation class** $o_V$ is a generator of the line $\Lambda^vV\subset V^{\otimes v}\subset H^{iv}(X^v,\mathbb Q)$. Here $\Lambda^v V$ is the image of the naive antisymmetrizer $\frac1{v!}\sum_\pi\mathrm{sgn}(\pi)\pi$ on $V^{\otimes v}$; for odd $i$ this agrees with the geometric symmetrizer $\frac1{v!}\sum_\pi\pi^*$. Put $o_i(X):=o_{H^i(X)}$.

**Proposition 2.2.**
(a) For every $X$ and every such $V$, $o_V$ is a Hodge class. In particular every $o_i(X)$ is a Hodge class on $X^{b_i}$.
(b) Every $g\in GL^{gr}(H)$ preserving $V$ acts on $o_V$ by $\det(g|_V)$.
(c) Let $i$ be odd. If $B(X)$ holds, then $o_i(X)$ and $o_{2n-i}(X)$ are algebraic. If only $C(X)$ holds, $o_{\max(i,2n-i)}(X)$ is algebraic.

*Proof.* (a) The antisymmetrizer is a morphism of Hodge structures, so $\Lambda^vV$ is a 1-dimensional rational Hodge structure of weight $iv$. This weight is even: if $i$ is odd then $v$ is even, by Hodge symmetry $h^{p,q}=h^{q,p}$ with $p\ne q$. If $L_{\mathbb C}=L^{p,q}$ is a line, then $L^{q,p}=\overline{L^{p,q}}\ne0$ forces $p=q$.

(b) This is immediate.

(c) Let $i<n$ be odd; the case $i=n$ is the same with $h^0$, and $i>n$ is symmetric. The form $\psi_i(x,y)=\int x\cup y\cup h^{n-i}$ on $H^i$ is alternating and nondegenerate (hard Lefschetz). The class $c_i:=(\pi_{2n-i}\times\pi_{2n-i})_*\Delta_*(h^{n-i})\in H^{2n-i}\otimes H^{2n-i}$ satisfies $\int(x\times y)\cup c_i=\pm\psi_i(x,y)$, so $c_i$ represents $\psi_i\in\Lambda^2(H^i)^\vee$, and it is algebraic under $C(X)$. The geometric symmetrization of $c_i^{\times b/2}$ on $X^{b}$ is a nonzero multiple of the Pfaffian $\psi_i^{\wedge b/2}$, which spans $\Lambda^b(H^i)^\vee\cong\Lambda^bH^{2n-i}$. Under $B(X)$ the inverse of $L^{n-i}$ is algebraic, and its $b$-th tensor power maps $o_{2n-i}$ to a nonzero multiple of $o_i$. $\square$

So in odd degree an orientation class is a polynomial in the polarization. In even degree it is not (Fact 0.4(O) versus (SO)), and this is where the problem lies.

**Proposition 2.3 (non-generation).** Let $S$ be a set of classes on powers of $X$ containing $[pt]$, $[\Delta_X]$ and the small diagonal $[\Delta_3]$. Let $\langle S\rangle$ be its closure under linear combinations, exterior products, cup products, and pull-back and push-forward along the maps $X^a\to X^b$ induced by maps of index sets $\{1..b\}\to\{1..a\}$ (projections, permutations, diagonals). Then $G_S$ fixes $\langle S\rangle$ pointwise. Consequently, if some $g\in G_S(\overline{\mathbb Q})$ preserves $V$ and has $\det(g|_V)\neq1$ (for instance a reflection of $V$), then $o_V\notin\langle S\rangle$.

*Proof.* As in the proof of 1.1(i), $g\in G_S$ is a ring automorphism of $H$ preserving $\int$. Hence each $g^{\otimes k}$ is a ring automorphism of $H^*(X^k)$ preserving $\int_{X^k}$. Exterior products, cup products, permutations and projections commute with $g$. Pull-back along a diagonal is a cup product of factors, so it commutes with $g$. Push-forwards are adjoint to pull-backs for $g$-invariant pairings, so they commute with $g$ as well. Hence the fixed space of $g$ is closed under all the operations, and it contains $S$. Finally, by 2.2(b), $g\,o_V=\det(g|_V)\,o_V\neq o_V$. $\square$

The set $S$ may contain the Künneth components, all diagonals, the polarization $h$, all algebraic classes on $X$ and on $X\times X$ (algebraic endomorphisms included), and indeed all algebraic classes on $X^k$ for any $k$ for which these are fixed by the reflection. So the literal top target (a) fails as soon as $G_S$ contains a reflection of an even-degree piece. Theorem A(5) gives the concrete instances: very general K3 surfaces and very general even-dimensional hypersurfaces.

**Proposition 2.4 (abelian varieties: no obstruction).** For an abelian variety $A$ and every $i$, $o_i(A)$ is a polynomial in divisor classes on powers of $A$. In particular it is algebraic.

*Proof.* Let $\varepsilon=c_1(\mathcal L)\in\Lambda^2H^1\subset H^1\otimes H^1$ for an ample $\mathcal L$. Then $\mathrm{Hg}(A)\subset Sp:=Sp(H^1,\varepsilon)\subset SL(H^1)$. As $GL(H^1)$-modules, $\Lambda^b(\Lambda^iH^1)\cong(\det H^1)^{\otimes c}$ for some $c$, so $Sp$ fixes $o_i(A)$. Let $F\in(H^1)^{\otimes ib}$ be the image of $o_i(A)$ under the $GL(H^1)$-equivariant inclusion $(\Lambda^iH^1)^{\otimes b}\subset(H^1)^{\otimes ib}$; $F$ is $Sp$-invariant. By Fact 0.4(Sp), $F$ is a combination of matchings of $\varepsilon$. Here $\varepsilon\in H^1\otimes H^1\subset H^2(A\times A)$ is a Hodge class, hence a divisor class (Lefschetz (1,1)). So $F$ is a polynomial in divisor classes on $A^{ib}$. Let $\delta:A^b\to A^{ib}$ be the diagonal on blocks of size $i$. Then $\delta^*$ is the cup product in each block, which maps antisymmetrized tensors of odd classes to their wedge product, so $\delta^*F=o_i(A)$. $\square$

**Proposition 2.5 (de Rham-absoluteness: consistency check for checklist item 1).** For every $X$, $o_n(X)$ is de Rham-absolute (weakly absolute in Voisin's sense): for every $\sigma$, $\sigma(t_{dR})=\pm t'_{dR}$ with $t'=o_n(X^\sigma)$. For every $i$, the de Rham conjugates of $o_i(X)$ are proportional to rational classes. Whether the $\ell$-adic signs agree with the de Rham sign (needed for absolute Hodge in Deligne's sense) is not proved here.

*Proof.* Normalize $t=o_n(X)=e_1\wedge\dots\wedge e_b$ for a $\mathbb Z$-basis $(e_j)$ of $H^n(X,\mathbb Z)/\mathrm{tors}$. Let $\psi_B$ be the cup-product pairing on $H^n$. Unimodularity gives $G:=\Lambda^b\psi_B(t,t)=\det(\psi_B(e_j,e_l))=\pm1$.

The de Rham form $\psi_{dR}=\mathrm{tr}_{dR}\circ\cup$ is algebraic and equals $(2\pi i)^{-n}\psi_B$ under comparison. The de Rham component of the Hodge class $t\in H^{nb}(X^b)(nb/2)$ is $t_{dR}=(2\pi i)^{nb/2}t$. Hence $\Lambda^b\psi_{dR}(t_{dR},t_{dR})=G$.

Let $\sigma\in\mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb C)$. The vector $\sigma(t_{dR})$ lies in the line $\Lambda^bH^n_{dR}(X^\sigma)$, because Künneth components and the action of permutations are algebraic. Write $\sigma(t_{dR})=c\,t'_{dR}$, where $t'$ is the normalized $o_n(X^\sigma)$. Applying $\sigma$ to the algebraic identity above gives $c^2G'=G$, with $G'=\pm1$ defined for $X^\sigma$ as $G$ is for $X$.

For $n$ even, the sign of $G$ is $(-1)^{\#\text{negative squares of }\psi_B}$. By the Hodge–Riemann relations this number is a function of the Hodge numbers. For $n$ odd, $G=+1$. Hodge numbers are invariant under $\sigma$. Hence $G=G'$, so $c=\pm1$, and $\sigma(t_{dR})$ is the de Rham component of the rational Hodge class $\pm t'$.

For $i\neq n$, run the same argument with $\psi_i=\int x\cup y\cup h^{n-i}$. It gives $c^2\in\mathbb Q^*$. $\square$

*Consistency with known results.* For hypersurfaces of even dimension, T. Saito [Sai12] identifies the Galois character on $\Lambda^{b}H^n_{\acute et}$ with the quadratic character of $\sqrt{\epsilon(n,d)\,\mathrm{disc}(f)}$. This is the behaviour of a cycle defined over the quadratic extension where the discriminant becomes a square, just as for the two rulings of an even-dimensional quadric. This is consistent with HC predicting that $o_n$ is algebraic.

## 3. Theorem A: the generic one-piece case (unconditional)

**Theorem A.** Let $X$ be smooth projective of dimension $n$, and let $\mathcal A:=\bigoplus_pA^p(X)$ be the space of algebraic classes on $X$. Assume:

**(H)** $H^*(X,\mathbb Q)=\mathcal A\oplus V$, where $V\subset H^n(X,\mathbb Q)$ is a sub-Hodge structure, and the restriction $\mathrm{Hg}(X)|_V$ is $Sp(V,\psi)$ if $n$ is odd, or $SO(V,\psi)$ with $r:=\dim V\ge3$ if $n$ is even. Here $\psi(x,y)=\int_Xx\cup y$.

Then:
1. $\mathcal A\perp V$ for Poincaré duality. The class $\pi_V:=[\Delta_X]-\sum_{j,l}g^{jl}a_j\times a_l$ is algebraic, where $(a_j)$ is a basis of $\mathcal A$ consisting of classes of cycles, $g_{jl}=\int a_j\cup a_l$, and $(g^{jl})=(g_{jl})^{-1}$. It lies in $V\otimes V$ and represents $\pm\psi^{-1}$.
2. Every Hodge class on $X^k$ is a $\mathbb Q$-linear combination of cup products of classes of the following kinds: $pr_a^*\alpha$ with $\alpha\in\mathcal A$; $pr_{ab}^*\pi_V$; and, only if $n$ is even and $k\ge r$, at most one factor $pr_J^*o_V$, where $pr_J:X^k\to X^r$ and $|J|=r$.
3. If $n$ is odd, HC holds for $X^k$ for every $k$.
4. If $n$ is even, HC holds for $X^k$ for $k<r$. For $k\ge r$: HC holds for $X^k$ $\iff$ $o_V$ is algebraic.
5. Suppose $n$ is even. Let $S$ consist of all algebraic classes on $X^k$ for $k<r$, together with $[pt]$ and all small diagonals. Then $o_V\notin\langle S\rangle$. In particular the Hodge classes on $X^r$ are **not** generated by Künneth components, diagonals, polarizations and algebraic endomorphisms, all of which lie in $S$.

*Proof.*

(1) Let $\alpha\in A^p(X)$. The map $v\mapsto\int\alpha\cup v$ is an $\mathrm{Hg}$-equivariant map $V\to\mathbb Q$. It vanishes, because $(V^\vee)^{\mathrm{Hg}}=0$. So $\mathcal A\perp V$, and Poincaré duality is nondegenerate on $\mathcal A$, while $\psi$ is nondegenerate on $V$. The correspondence $\pi_{\mathcal A}=\sum g^{jl}a_j\times a_l$ acts as the projection onto $\mathcal A$ with kernel $V$. Hence $\pi_V$ acts as the projection onto $V$ with kernel $\mathcal A$. Write $\pi_V=\sum_kv^k\otimes v_k$, where $(v_k)$ is a basis of $V$. Each $v^k$ is PD-orthogonal to $\mathcal A$, hence lies in $V$, and $\int v^k\cup v_l=\pm\delta_{kl}$.

(2) $\mathrm{Hg}$ acts trivially on $\mathcal A$ (Fact 0.1). Write $H^{\otimes k}=\bigoplus_J\mathcal A^{\otimes J^c}\otimes V^{\otimes J}$, where $J$ is the set of slots carrying $V$. The Hodge classes are then $\bigoplus_J\mathcal A^{\otimes J^c}\otimes(V^{\otimes J})^{\mathrm{Hg}}$. Apply Fact 0.4 (Sp) or (SO) to each $(V^{\otimes J})^{\mathrm{Hg}}$. Under Künneth, $\psi^{-1}$ placed in slots $a,b$ corresponds to $\pm pr_{ab}^*\pi_V$, and $\delta_J$ corresponds to $\pm pr_J^*o_V$.

(3), (4) The classes $pr_a^*\alpha$ and $pr_{ab}^*\pi_V$ are algebraic by (1). For $k<r$ no $o_V$ factor occurs. Conversely, suppose HC holds for $X^k$ with $k\ge r$. Then $o_V\times[pt]^{\times(k-r)}$ is algebraic, and pushing forward along $X^k\to X^r$ gives $o_V$.

(5) Let $O(V)$ act on $H$ by the identity on $\mathcal A$. It fixes $\mathcal A$ and $\pi_V$. By (2) and (4), the algebraic classes on $X^k$ with $k<r$ are combinations of $pr^*\alpha$ and $pr^*\pi_V$, so $O(V)$ fixes them too. It also preserves the cup product. Indeed, $\mathcal A$ is a subring. For $\alpha\in A^p$ with $p>0$, the map $v\mapsto\alpha\cup v$ is an $\mathrm{Hg}$-map from $V$ to $H^{n+2p}$. That target lies in $\mathcal A$ and is a trivial $\mathrm{Hg}$-module, so the map is $0$. Finally $v\cup w=\psi(v,w)\,[pt]$. Hence $O(V)\subset G_S$, as in Proposition 2.3. A reflection of $V$ has determinant $-1$, and Proposition 2.3 applies. $\square$

**Corollary 3.1 (surfaces with $p_g=1$; rung (b)).** Let $S$ be a smooth projective surface with $p_g=1$, $q=0$, and $E:=\mathrm{End}_{HS}(T)=\mathbb Q$, where $T:=NS(S)_{\mathbb Q}^\perp\subset H^2$ and $r:=\dim T$. Then $r\ge3$, and (H) holds with $\mathcal A=H^0\oplus NS_{\mathbb Q}\oplus H^4$ and $V=T$. Hence:
- HC holds for $S^k$ for all $k<r$.
- HC holds for $S^k$ for some (equivalently, for every) $k\ge r$ $\iff$ $o_T\in H^{2r}(S^r)$ is algebraic.
- $o_T$ is not in the span generated by diagonals, divisors and algebraic classes on $S^k$ for $k<r$.

For K3 surfaces this is, in substance, due to Varesco [Var24]. He corrected the totally real case of [RM08, Prop. 5.2], which had overlooked these determinant classes. Our proof is the same for every surface with $p_g=1$, $q=0$.

*Proof.* Since $q=0$, we have $H^1=H^3=0$. By Lefschetz (1,1), the algebraic classes are $H^0\oplus NS_{\mathbb Q}\oplus H^4$. By the Hodge index theorem, $H^2=NS_{\mathbb Q}\oplus T$. The Hodge structure $T$ is irreducible, polarized and of K3 type, so Zarhin gives $\mathrm{Hg}(T)=SO(T)$. Since $\mathrm{Hg}(S)$ acts trivially on $\mathcal A$, it follows that $\mathrm{Hg}(S)|_T=SO(T)$. If $r=2$, then $SO(T)$ is a torus, so its commutant in $\mathrm{End}(T)$ is a quadratic field, contradicting $E=\mathbb Q$. Hence $r\ge3$. $\square$

**Corollary 3.2 (CM case; known [RM08] + [Bus19]).** If $S$ is a K3 surface and $E$ is a CM field, then HC holds for $S^k$ for every $k$, and in particular $o_T$ is algebraic. Indeed $\mathrm{Hg}=U_E(T)$ (Fact 0.6), and over $\mathbb C$ we have $U_E(T)\cong\prod_{\sigma\in\Phi}GL(T_\sigma)$, acting on $T_{\bar\sigma}\cong T_\sigma^\vee$. By the first fundamental theorem for $GL$, all invariants are spanned by products of degree-two invariants. These are the classes $\gamma_e$ ($e\in E$) on $S\times S$. They are algebraic because the norm-one elements of $E$ are Hodge isometries, which are algebraic by Buskin's theorem, and they span $E$ (see attack 04, Remark 2.3).

**Remark 3.3 (exactly where Buskin and Kuga–Satake enter).**
- **$E=\mathbb Q$.** Buskin's theorem is *not needed*: the degree-two Hodge classes on $S\times S$ are spanned by $NS\otimes NS$ and $\pi_T$, which are trivially algebraic. The only missing class is $o_T$, and the relevant input is Kuga–Satake (Theorem B).
- **$E$ CM.** Buskin is needed, and it suffices (Corollary 3.2). Kuga–Satake is not needed.
- **$E$ totally real, $E\ne\mathbb Q$.** Both kinds of class are needed. The RM classes $\gamma_e$ are not similitudes, so Buskin does not reach them (attack 04, Theorem A). The $E$-determinant classes in $\Lambda^m_ET$ are needed as well. Not treated here.
- **Products of different K3 surfaces with isogenous $T$'s.** Buskin is needed for Hodge isometries $T(S_1)\to T(S_2)$. Similitudes with non-square multiplier are not covered by his theorem.

**Corollary 3.4 (very general hypersurfaces).** Let $n\ge1$ and $d\ge3$, with $(n,d)\ne(2,3)$. Let $X\subset\mathbb P^{n+1}$ be a very general smooth hypersurface of degree $d$, and let $V=H^n_{prim}(X,\mathbb Q)$. Then (H) holds with $\mathcal A=\mathbb Q[h]/(h^{n+1})$. Consequently:
- if $n$ is odd, HC holds for $X^k$ for every $k$;
- if $n$ is even, HC holds for $X^k$ for $k<r=b_n-1$, and HC for all powers is equivalent to the algebraicity of $o_V$, which is not in $\langle S\rangle$.

Examples: for the very general quartic surface $r=21$; for the very general cubic fourfold $r=22$.

*Proof.* By the Lefschetz hyperplane theorem, $H=\mathbb Q[h]/(h^{n+1})\oplus V$. The Zariski closure of the monodromy group of the universal family on $V$ is $Sp(V)$ if $n$ is odd and $O(V)$ if $n$ is even: see [Del80, 4.4.1], and, for infiniteness of the monodromy when $n$ is even, $d\ge3$ and $(n,d)\ne(2,3)$, [Bea86]. By André [And92, Thm. 1], for $X$ outside a countable union of proper closed subsets, the identity component of this closure is contained in $\mathrm{MT}(V)^{der}\subset\mathrm{Hg}(V)$. Since $\mathrm{Hg}(V)$ is connected and preserves $\psi$, it equals $Sp(V)$, resp. $SO(V)$. Hence $V^{\mathrm{Hg}}=0$, so the algebraic classes on $X$ are exactly $\mathbb Q[h]$. Finally, $r=((d-1)^{n+2}+(d-1))/d\ge6$ for $n$ even. $\square$

The odd-dimensional case is an immediate combination of known theorems. We do not claim it as new, although we could not locate it stated in the literature.

**Corollary 3.5 (parity criterion).** In Theorem A, suppose $n$ is even and $r$ is odd, as for the very general K3 surface ($r=21$). Then HC holds for all powers of $X$ $\iff$ there is an algebraic class on some $X^k$ whose component in some summand $\mathcal A^{\otimes J^c}\otimes V^{\otimes J}$ with $|J|$ odd is nonzero.

*Proof.* "$\Rightarrow$": take $o_V$ itself ($|J|=r$ is odd).

"$\Leftarrow$": the projectors $\pi_{\mathcal A}$ and $\pi_V$ are algebraic, so the chosen component is algebraic. Pair its $\mathcal A$-slots with suitable algebraic classes and push forward. This gives a nonzero algebraic $t\in(V^{\otimes j})^{SO}$ with $j$ odd. By Fact 0.4, $t$ is a combination of tensors $\delta_{J'}\otimes\psi^{-1}_\mu$; pure matchings cannot occur because $j$ is odd. The invariant pairing on $(V^{\otimes j})^{SO}$ is nondegenerate, since $SO$ is reductive. So $\langle t,\delta_{J'}\otimes\psi^{-1}_\mu\rangle\neq0$ for some $(J',\mu)$. Contract $t$ along $\mu$; the contraction of slots $a,b$ is $t\mapsto pr_*(t\cup pr_{ab}^*[\Delta])$, an algebraic operation. The result $u$ is algebraic, lies in $\mathbb Q\,\delta_{J'}$, and satisfies $\langle u,\delta_{J'}\rangle\neq0$. Hence $o_V$ is algebraic. $\square$

**Remark 3.6 (products of very general K3 surfaces).** Apply André's theorem to the product family over $M^m$. Its monodromy closure is $\prod O(T_i)$, so for very general $(S_1,\dots,S_m)$ one gets $\mathrm{Hg}=\prod SO(T_i)$. The invariants are then tensor products of the invariants of the factors. Hence HC for all products $\prod S_i^{k_i}$ holds $\iff$ each $o_{T_i}$ is algebraic, and this reduces to the single-surface problem.

---

## 4. Theorem B: Kuga–Satake implies algebraicity of the orientation class

**Set-up.** Let $S$ be a smooth projective surface with $p_g(S)=1$. Put $T=T(S)_{\mathbb Q}$, let $q$ be the intersection form, and $r=\dim T$. Let $C=C(T,q)$ be the Clifford algebra, with relations $x^2=q(x)$, grading $C=C^+\oplus C^-$, and $\dim C=2^r$. For $c\in C$ write $L_c$ and $R_c$ for left and right multiplication by $c$.

Let $e_1,e_2$ be a $q$-orthonormal basis of the positive plane $P=T_{\mathbb R}\cap(T^{2,0}\oplus T^{0,2})$, and put $J=e_1e_2\in C^+_{\mathbb R}$, so $J^2=-1$. The **Kuga–Satake Hodge structure** on $C$ has weight one, with complex structure $L_J$. It is polarizable [Del72, §4], [vG00], [Huy16, Ch. 4]. So $C\cong H^1(A',\mathbb Q)$ for an abelian variety $A'$, isogenous to the square of the usual Kuga–Satake variety $A$, whose $H^1$ is $C^+$. Put $g=\dim A'=2^{r-1}$. We use three facts.
- **(KS1)** $R_c\in\mathrm{End}_{HS}(C)$ for every $c\in C$.
- **(KS2)** If $c\in C$ commutes with $C^+$ (hence with $J$), then $L_c\in\mathrm{End}_{HS}(C)$, since $L_c$ commutes with $L_J$.
- **(KS3)** The map $x\mapsto L_x$ is a morphism of Hodge structures $T(1)\to\mathrm{End}(H^1(A'))$. Check: $h_C(a+bi)=L_u$ with $u=a+bJ$, and $L_uL_xL_u^{-1}=L_{uxu^{-1}}$. For $x\perp P$ one has $uxu^{-1}=x$. For $x\in P$, $Jx=-xJ$ gives $uxu^{-1}=x(a-bJ)^2/(a^2+b^2)$, which is a rotation of $P$ by $\mp2\arg(a+bi)$. This is the action of $h_{T(1)}$ (for the standard choice of sign of $J$).

For $\varphi\in\mathrm{End}(H^1(A'))$, let $[\varphi]\in H^{2g-1}(A')\otimes H^1(A')\subset H^{2g}(A'\times A')$ be the class that acts as $\varphi$ on $H^1$ and as $0$ on all other $H^j$.

**Hypothesis KS(S).** There is $\Gamma_\kappa\in A^{g+1}(S\times A'\times A')$ such that $(\Gamma_\kappa)_*x=[L_x]$ for every $x\in T$.

This is implied by the usual Kuga–Satake Hodge conjecture [vG00], [Var24], which asks that the Hodge class realizing $x\mapsto(y\mapsto xyv_0)$, $T(1)\to\mathrm{End}(C^+)$, be algebraic. Indeed, write $C=C^+\oplus C^+v_0$; this decomposition is induced by an isogeny $A\times A\to A'$. In it, $L_x=\begin{pmatrix}0&\varphi_x\\ q(v_0)^{-1}\varphi_x&0\end{pmatrix}$ with $\varphi_x(y)=xyv_0$. The Künneth projectors of abelian varieties are algebraic.

**Theorem B.** If $S$ is a smooth projective surface with $p_g=1$ and KS(S) holds, then $o_T$ is algebraic, for every value of $\rho(S)$. If moreover $q(S)=0$ and $\mathrm{End}_{HS}(T)=\mathbb Q$, then HC holds for $S^k$ for every $k$.

*Proof.* Choose a $q$-orthogonal rational basis $e_1,\dots,e_r$ of $T$, put $a_i=q(e_i)\in\mathbb Q^*$, and let $\omega=e_1\cdots e_r\in C$ be the volume element.

*Step 1: $L_\omega$ is an algebraic endomorphism of $A'$.* Distinct $e_i$ anticommute, so $e_i\omega=(-1)^{r-1}\omega e_i$. Hence $\omega$ commutes with $C^+$. By (KS2), $L_\omega$ commutes with $L_J$, so $L_\omega\in\mathrm{End}_{HS}(H^1(A'))=\mathrm{End}^0(A')$. The class $[L_\omega]$ is the $H^{2g-1}\otimes H^1$ Künneth component of the class of the graph of the corresponding endomorphism. It is therefore algebraic (Fact 0.3).

*Step 2: an algebraic correspondence realizing Clifford multiplication.* Let $c_r\in A^*((A'\times A')^r\times A'\times A')$ be the composition-of-correspondences class (a partial diagonal). It sends $[\varphi_1]\times\cdots\times[\varphi_r]$ to $\pm[\varphi_1\circ\cdots\circ\varphi_r]$. Put $\Theta:=c_r\circ(\Gamma_\kappa\circ\pi_T)^{\times r}$; it is algebraic. All classes involved have even degree, so no Koszul signs arise from the exterior product, and for $x_i\in T$
$$\Theta_*(x_1\times\cdots\times x_r)=\pm[L_{x_1}\circ\cdots\circ L_{x_r}]=\pm[L_{x_1\cdots x_r}].$$
Moreover $\Theta_*$ vanishes on the Künneth components of $H^*(S^r)$ other than $T^{\otimes r}$.

*Step 3: the trace pairing.* Let $(f_a)$ be a basis of $H^1(A')$ with PD-dual basis $(f^a)$. Writing $[\varphi]=\sum\varphi_{ab}f^b\times f_a$, a direct computation gives
$$\int_{A'\times A'}[\varphi]\cup{}^t[\varphi']=\pm\,\mathrm{tr}(\varphi\circ\varphi'),$$
with a universal sign [Kle68, §1.3]. Put $w:=(\pi_T^{\times r})_*({}^t\Theta)_*({}^t[L_\omega])$; it is algebraic. By Fact 0.3, for every $u\in T^{\otimes r}$,
$$\int_{S^r}u\cup w=\pm\int_{A'\times A'}\Theta_*u\cup{}^t[L_\omega]=\pm\,\mathrm{tr}_C\big(L_{\Lambda(u)\omega}\big)=\pm\,2^r\,[\Lambda(u)\omega]_0 ,$$
where $\Lambda(x_1\otimes\cdots\otimes x_r)=x_1\cdots x_r$ and $[c]_0$ is the scalar coefficient of $c$. The last equality holds because $\mathrm{tr}(L_{e_K})=0$ for every monomial $e_K$ with $K\ne\emptyset$: left multiplication by $e_K$ permutes the monomial basis without fixed points, up to scalars.

*Step 4: evaluation.* Take $u=e_{i_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{i_r}$. Then $e_{i_1}\cdots e_{i_r}$ equals $\pm(\prod a)\,e_K$, where $K$ is the set of indices occurring an odd number of times. If $(i_1,\dots,i_r)$ is not a permutation, some index $j\notin K$, so $e_K\omega$ is not a scalar and $[\Lambda(u)\omega]_0=0$. If $(i_\bullet)=\pi$ is a permutation, then $[\Lambda(u)\omega]_0=\mathrm{sgn}(\pi)\,\omega^2$, with $\omega^2=(-1)^{r(r-1)/2}\prod a_i\neq0$. So $u\mapsto\int u\cup w$ is a nonzero multiple of the determinant functional $\det(e^i(u_j))$ on $T^{\otimes r}$.

The pairing $\int_{S^r}$ restricted to $T^{\otimes r}$ is $q^{\otimes r}$, and $w\in T^{\otimes r}$. Hence $w$ is the $q^{\otimes r}$-dual of that functional, a nonzero element of $\Lambda^rT$. So $w=c\,o_T$ with $c\ne0$, and $o_T$ is algebraic. The last assertion follows from Corollary 3.1. $\square$

**Remark 4.1 (relation to the literature; what is and is not new).** Take a family of K3 surfaces of generic Picard number 16 with algebraic Kuga–Satake correspondence. Varesco [Var24] reduces HC for all powers of its members to HC for powers of the Kuga–Satake variety. By Lombardo [Lom01], that variety is a power of an abelian fourfold of Weil type with discriminant 1. The Kuga–Satake algebraicity in such families is established in [Flo26] (arXiv:2210.02948); HC for all powers then follows from [Var24, Thm. 0.2], which builds on Markman's work. This route needs the Hodge conjecture for the exceptional classes on powers of the Kuga–Satake variety, which is available only in such special cases. Theorem B needs only the single endomorphism $L_\omega$, so it applies for every Picard number.

The conceptual point is this. Reversing the orientation of $T$ replaces $\omega$ by $-\omega$. The Kuga–Satake variety "knows" the orientation through an endomorphism, and endomorphisms are always algebraic.

To our knowledge this general implication is not stated in the literature. We could read only abstracts and secondary descriptions of [Var24], since arXiv is blocked here. *No new unconditional case follows*: KS(S) is known only for some families with $\rho\ge16$ [Par88], [Flo26] ([Lom01] identifies the Kuga–Satake varieties; [Var24] assumes KS), and in many cases with $\rho\ge17$ [Mor84]. In all of these the conclusion was already known.

---

## 5. Theorem C: unconditional reduction to finitely many primitive classes (rung (c))

Put $W:=H^\vee$ and $N:=\dim H$. Multilinear functions on $W^{\oplus k}$ are elements of $H^{\otimes k}$, and $\mathrm{Hg}(X)$ acts compatibly. Let $f$ be a multihomogeneous polynomial on $W^{\oplus N}$ of multidegree $(d_1,\dots,d_N)$ and total degree $d$. Its **full polarization** $P(f)\in\bigotimes_l\mathrm{Sym}^{d_l}H\subset H^{\otimes d}$ is the multilinear form on $W^d$, symmetric in each block, with $P(f)(w_1^{(d_1)},\dots,w_N^{(d_N)})=(\prod d_l!)\,f(w_1,\dots,w_N)$.

**Theorem C.** Let $X$ be any smooth projective variety. Let $f_1,\dots,f_M$ be multihomogeneous generators of $\mathbb Q[W^{\oplus N}]^{\mathrm{Hg}(X)}$; there are finitely many, by Hilbert's theorem, since $\mathrm{Hg}$ is reductive. Let $t_1,\dots,t_R$ be the Künneth-homogeneous components, i.e. the components in the summands $H^{a_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes H^{a_d}$, of the tensors $P(f_j)$. Each $t_\nu$ is a Hodge class on $X^{d(\nu)}$. Then, for every $k$, the Hodge classes on $X^k$ are spanned by the classes $\sigma^*(t_{\nu_1}\times\cdots\times t_{\nu_s})$, where $\sum d(\nu_i)=k$ and $\sigma$ permutes the factors. Consequently, HC holds for all powers of $X$ $\iff$ $t_1,\dots,t_R$ are algebraic.

*Proof.* Each $P(f_j)$ is $\mathrm{Hg}$-invariant, and $\mathrm{Hg}\subset GL^{gr}(H)$ preserves the Künneth multigrading. So each $t_\nu$ is invariant, hence a Hodge class (Fact 0.1).

Let $F$ be a Hodge class on $X^k$, viewed as an invariant multilinear function of $w_1,\dots,w_k$, and put $m=\max(k,N)$. By Fact 0.5 (trivially if $m=N$), $F$ is a polynomial in multihomogeneous polarizations of the $f_j$ on $W^{\oplus m}$. Take the component of multidegree $(1^k,0^{m-k})$. It is a combination of products $g_1\cdots g_s$ of polarizations, and each $g_i$ is multilinear in a set $L_i$ of variables, with the $L_i$ disjoint and $\bigsqcup L_i=\{1,\dots,k\}$. Expanding $f_j(\sum_lA_{1l}w_l,\dots)$ by multilinearity of $P(f_j)$ shows that such a $g_i$ is a combination of $P(f_j)(w_{\beta(1)},\dots,w_{\beta(d)})$ over bijections $\beta:\{1..d\}\to L_i$. In tensor language, it is a combination of copies of $P(f_j)$ with relabelled slots. So $F$ lies in the span of naively permuted tensor products of the $P(f_j)$. Now decompose into Künneth-homogeneous components. On a homogeneous tensor, the naive permutation differs from the geometric one $\sigma^*$ only by a sign. This gives the spanning statement.

For the equivalence: "$\Leftarrow$" holds because exterior products and permutations preserve algebraicity. "$\Rightarrow$" holds because each $t_\nu$ is a Hodge class. $\square$

**Remarks.** (i) Theorem C needs no standard conjecture. It uses reductivity of $\mathrm{Hg}$ (projectivity) and characteristic 0 (polarization involves division by factorials). (ii) The list is explicit relative to $\mathrm{Hg}(X)$, which is not computable in general. In the situation of Theorem A, the list can be taken to be $\{\alpha\in\mathcal A\}\cup\{\pi_V\}\cup\{o_V\}$. (iii) Effective bounds for the degrees $d(\nu)$ can be extracted from known degree bounds for generators of invariant rings. We did not verify the published bounds and state none.

---

## 6. K3 surfaces: the orientation class as a variational problem

Fix $d\ge1$. Let $B$ be an irreducible smooth quasi-projective variety carrying a smooth projective family $f:\mathcal S\to B$ of $2d$-polarized K3 surfaces in which every $2d$-polarized K3 surface occurs as a fibre. For instance, take the open part of a Hilbert scheme parametrizing K3 surfaces embedded by $|3h|$, a $PGL$-torsor over the smooth irreducible moduli stack [Huy16, Ch. 5]. Let $\mathbb L:=\Lambda^{21}R^2_{prim}f_*\mathbb Q$, a rank-one local system, and let $\tilde B\to B$ be the connected étale cover of degree $\le2$ that trivializes it, which we call the *orientation cover*. Let $o\in H^0(\tilde B,\mathbb L)$ be a generator. At $s\in\tilde B$, $o_s\in H^{42}(S_s^{21},\mathbb Q)$ is a Hodge class (Proposition 2.2). The monodromy contains Picard–Lefschetz reflections in $(-2)$-classes orthogonal to $h$, so $\tilde B\neq B$.

**Lemma 6.1 (no cycle defined over the moduli space sees the orientation).** Let $B'\to B$ be a connected étale cover whose monodromy group contains an element acting on $h^\perp$ with determinant $-1$; for example $B'=B$. Let $Z$ be an algebraic cycle on the fibre power $\mathcal S^k_{B'}$. Then, at a very general point $s$, the class $[Z_s]$ is $O(T_s)$-invariant. In particular its component in the $o$-type summand of Theorem A(2) is zero. Hence any family of cycles representing $o$ at the very general point is defined over a cover through which $\tilde B\to B$ factors.

*Proof.* The class $[Z_s]$ is the restriction of a global class, so it is monodromy-invariant. At a very general $s$ we have $NS=\mathbb Qh$ and $T_s=h^\perp$. The monodromy fixes $h$, $H^0$ and $H^4$, and acts on $T_s$ through $O(T_s)$. The Hodge classes split canonically into $O(T_s)$-invariants (matchings) and the $\det$-isotypic part ($o$-type terms). An element with $\det=-1$ acts by $-1$ on the latter, so the $o$-type component of $[Z_s]$ vanishes. $\square$

**Proposition 6.2.** The following are equivalent.
1. HC holds for $S^k$, for all $k$, where $S$ is a very general $2d$-polarized K3 surface.
2. $o_s$ is algebraic for very general $s\in\tilde B$.
3. There exist a relatively ample class and $D$ such that, for **every** $s\in\tilde B$, $o_s$ is a rational multiple of $[Z_s^+]-[Z_s^-]$, with $Z^\pm_s$ effective cycles of degree $\le D$.
4. HC holds for $S^k$, for all $k$, for **every** $2d$-polarized K3 surface $S$ with $\mathrm{End}_{HS}(T(S))=\mathbb Q$.
5. There exist $D$ and a Zariski-dense set $\Sigma\subset\tilde B$ of points whose fibres have CM, such that $o_s$, for $s\in\Sigma$, is a rational multiple of a difference of effective cycles of degree $\le D$.

Without degree control, $o_s$ *is* algebraic at every CM point (Corollary 3.2).

*Proof.* The very general fibre has $\rho=1$, $T=h^\perp$, and $\mathrm{Hg}=SO(T)$ (monodromy and [And92]), so $E=\mathbb Q$.

(1)$\Leftrightarrow$(2). Apply Corollary 3.1 with $o_T=o_s$.

(2)$\Rightarrow$(3). Let $\mathcal Y=\mathcal S^{21}\times_B\tilde B\to\tilde B$. Fix a pair of components $W^\pm$ of the relative Chow variety of $\mathcal Y/\tilde B$ (countably many pairs) and $\lambda\in\mathbb Q^*$. The locus in $W^+\times_{\tilde B}W^-$ where $[Z^+]-[Z^-]=\lambda o$ is a union of connected components: classes of algebraic families of cycles are flat, and $o$ is flat. Its image in $\tilde B$ is closed, since Chow varieties of bounded degree are proper over the base [Kol96, Ch. I]. By (2), countably many such closed sets cover the complement of a countable union of proper closed subsets. By Baire, one of them is all of $\tilde B$.

(3)$\Rightarrow$(4). Let $S_0$ have $\mathrm{End}(T_0)=\mathbb Q$. Let $N=h^\perp\cap NS(S_0)_{\mathbb Q}$; it is spanned by divisor classes and $q|_N$ is negative definite. Then $o_{s_0}$ spans $\Lambda^{21}(N\oplus T_0)=\Lambda^{\dim N}N\otimes\Lambda^{r_0}T_0$. Contracting with the dual basis of $N$ is an algebraic operation: cup with pulled-back divisor classes, then push forward. It yields a nonzero multiple of $o_{T_0}$, which is therefore algebraic. Now apply Corollary 3.1.

(4)$\Rightarrow$(1) is trivial.

(3)$\Rightarrow$(5). CM points are dense in $\tilde B$.

(5)$\Rightarrow$(3). Chow varieties of degree $\le D$ have finitely many components. On each component, $\lambda$ is constant by flatness, so only finitely many values of $\lambda$ occur. Some component therefore has image containing a Zariski-dense subset of $\Sigma$. That image is constructible and dense, so it contains an open dense subset, and it is closed by properness. Hence it is all of $\tilde B$. $\square$

*Meaning.* By Lemma 6.1 and Proposition 6.2, rung (b) for very general K3 surfaces is exactly the problem of producing, over the orientation cover of moduli, one bounded family of cycles. Seeds exist at every CM point. What is missing is control of their degrees. The cycles produced by Buskin's proof (via twisted derived equivalences and deformation) come with no degree bound. This is mechanism M2/M5 of docs/03 applied to one explicit flat class.

---

## 7. GAPS

- **G1 (main gap: top of rung (b)).** We need the following statement. *Let $S$ be a K3 surface (or any surface with $p_g=1$, $q=0$) with $\mathrm{End}_{HS}(T)=\mathbb Q$, for instance the very general $2d$-polarized K3 surface ($r=21$). Then some algebraic cycle on $S^r$ has a nonzero component in $\Lambda^rT\subset H^{2r}(S^r)$.*
  - *Why it is needed.* By Corollary 3.1 it is equivalent to HC for all powers of $S$, and it is the only missing class.
  - *Equivalent forms.* Corollary 3.5 (an algebraic class with odd $T$-degree); Proposition 6.2(2) and (5) (bounded-degree seeds at CM points).
  - *Why we cannot prove it.* Lemma 6.1 shows that no family of cycles defined over the moduli space (Hilbert schemes, tautological or universal sheaves, moduli of sheaves, Fano-type constructions in families) can work. The construction must depend on an orientation of $T$, i.e. live over the orientation cover. The only orientation-sensitive algebraic structure we know is the Kuga–Satake one (Theorem B), whose algebraicity is open in general and is known only for some families with $\rho\ge16$ and many cases with $\rho\ge17$. The seeds at CM points (Corollary 3.2) come from Buskin's theorem without any degree bound.
- **G2 (hypersurfaces).** For very general hypersurfaces of even dimension, the class $o_V$ is open. Examples: the cubic fourfold ($r=22$), quintic surfaces, sextic surfaces. We did not check whether HC is known for the relevant powers of Fermat hypersurfaces, which would provide seeds for a §6-type argument.
- **G3 (real multiplication).** $E$ totally real, $E\neq\mathbb Q$: both the RM classes (attack 04) and the $E$-determinant classes in $\Lambda^m_ET$ are open. We do not treat this case, and Theorem B does not reach the RM classes.
- **G4 ($q(S)>0$).** Then $\mathrm{Hg}(S)\subset\mathrm{Hg}(\mathrm{Alb})\times SO(T)$. Determining it requires a Goursat analysis; the cases $r=3,4$ need care because of $SO(3)\cong PGL_2$ and $SO(4)$. Not done.
- **G5 (several pieces).** For the general "generic" case, where $H$ has several orthogonal, unitary or symplectic pieces related by Goursat, we give only the $\pi_0$ formalism (Proposition 1.2, under $B$). There is no explicit description of $\pi_0(G_S)$.
- **G6 (effectivity).** The list in Theorem C is explicit only relative to $\mathrm{Hg}(X)$, and we state no degree bound.
- **G7 (literature checks).** arXiv and two other hosts are blocked from this session, and the web-search budget ran out before the end. [Var24] was consulted only through abstracts and secondary descriptions. Our statement that Theorem B (for arbitrary Picard number), Theorem A beyond K3 surfaces, Corollary 3.4, Theorem C and Proposition 6.2 (except its step (3)$\Rightarrow$(4), which is [Var24, Prop. 2.22]) are not in the literature rests on these partial checks. Theorem numbers in [GW09] and [Kle68] were not verified. An October 2026 OpenAI manuscript is listed in docs/02 §2.2 as **[unverified]**; we use nothing from it.

---

## 8. Checklist (docs/03, §3.4)

1. **Absoluteness.** Proposition 2.5 proves that middle-degree orientation classes are de Rham-absolute (the adelic component is not treated), and that the de Rham conjugates of the others are proportional to rational classes. This is the consistency check for the one new kind of class singled out here. Nothing else is claimed; every other class handled here lies in the span of algebraic classes.
2. **Lefschetz $B$.** It is used only as a hypothesis in Propositions 1.1, 1.2 and 2.2(c). Theorems A, B, C and §6 do not use it; $B$ holds for surfaces and hypersurfaces anyway. Nothing here proves $B$.
3. **Variational HC.** Proposition 6.2 makes rung (b) for K3 surfaces a bounded-degree/variational statement about one flat class. It does not prove it.
4. **Open special cases.** None is settled. CM K3 surfaces were already known; real multiplication is untouched; $o_V$ for hypersurfaces is open.
5. **$\mathbb Q$-coefficients.** They are essential at several points:
   - the projector $\pi_{\mathcal A}$ uses the inverse Gram matrix, with denominators $\mathrm{disc}(NS)$, resp. $d$;
   - the first fundamental theorems give $\mathbb Q$-spans, and $\Lambda^rT$ is only a rational line;
   - Tannakian semisimplicity (Proposition 1.1) is a phenomenon over a field;
   - Weyl polarization divides by factorials (Theorem C);
   - Theorem B produces $2^r\omega^2\,o_T$, not $o_T$.

   Every conclusion is a statement about $\mathbb Q$-spans. **The integral Hodge conjecture is neither claimed nor implied:** nothing here controls $H^*(X^k,\mathbb Z)\cap\mathrm{Hdg}$.

   **Projectivity** is used at four points:
   - (i) reductivity of $\mathrm{Hg}$ through polarizability, which is used in Fact 0.2, Proposition 1.1 and Theorem C;
   - (ii) in (H), $\mathcal A$ must consist of classes of algebraic cycles: on a projective surface $NS_{\mathbb Q}$ is spanned by divisors (twist by an ample class), whereas on a Kähler surface Hodge classes in $H^2$ need not be classes of analytic cycles (docs/01 §1.3);
   - (iii) the Kuga–Satake variety is an abelian variety only because $T$ is polarized, and only then are its endomorphisms algebraic (Theorem B);
   - (iv) Chow varieties are used in §6.

   **Kähler test.** Our arguments only express Hodge classes as combinations of products of explicit cycle classes: diagonals, points, divisors, graphs of endomorphisms. On a compact Kähler manifold where these classes are analytic, the same conclusions hold and are *true*. Voisin's tori violate (H): their Hodge classes are not in the span of diagonals and analytic classes. So no false variant follows. No step manufactures a cycle out of transcendental data; the only new algebraicity, Theorem B, is derived from the hypothesis KS(S).
